implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use Point Praise at Practice whenever you want to encourage a child. Remove one vague compliment, then name the behavior, cue, or repair step the child can repeat. Keep affection steady, but make praise point at practice.

ifThenPlans.context: If a compliment would name identity before behavior
ifThenPlans.plan: If the compliment starts with who the child is, then use Point Praise at Practice. Name the act they can repeat before adding any warm words.

ifThenPlans.context: If a child is staring at the thing they want
ifThenPlans.plan: If the reward has all their attention, then use Point Praise at Practice. Change the cue first, then praise the looking-away strategy.

ifThenPlans.context: If a school win sits beside an unfixed hurt
ifThenPlans.plan: If achievement is masking a social miss, then use Point Praise at Practice. Praise the work and attach repair as the next practice step.

ifThenPlans.context: If a rule starts to feel cold in your mouth
ifThenPlans.plan: If the routine sounds harsh, then use Point Praise at Practice. Say the affection plainly and keep the rule steady enough to help.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you reach for broad praise, move one distraction out of sight, remove the vague line, and praise the repeatable act.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, stage one real homework, chore, or repair reset. Before it begins, move the easiest distraction out of sight, then rehearse Point Praise at Practice when the child waits, starts, or repairs.

memorableLines.text: Praise is a mirror, not a motor.
Waiting gets easier when attention has somewhere else to go.
Warm rules beat loud praise.

chapters.title: The Perfect Storm of Dieting
chapters.hook: 1 bite can make a diet feel ruined, what if the bite is not the failure but the bad rule?
chapters.counterintuition: A diet can be sincere and still be built to snap. When one lapse ruins the day, shame has joined hunger at the table.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next food cue, write one plain rule sentence and read it aloud. Add one tally before you choose: hunger, cue, or shame.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Food control lasts when you make meals routine, lower cues, monitor calmly, and keep one lapse from becoming proof that the whole day is lost.

breakdown.fastRead: Why does Clara feel more at risk after one bite than before the diet began? The shake is gone, the plate is still there, and the rule now sounds broken. A brittle rule turns a bite into a verdict. Dieting is hard because food is not a drug you can quit. You have to meet it at breakfast, lunch, dinner, birthdays, and bad days. The useful move is not to diet harder after shame starts talking. Count the cue, lower the cue, and make the next meal ordinary.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism starts before the fork moves. A visible snack can pull attention, hunger can make the snack louder, and a strict rule can make one slip feel final. In restrained-eating work by C. Peter Herman and Janet Polivy, some restrained eaters ate more after a high-calorie preload. The name for that pattern is counterregulation: the broken rule invites the very eating it was meant to stop.

You have felt a mild version of it when a single cookie changes the story from "I am on plan" to "I ruined the day." That story is the trap. Shame promises discipline, but it often makes repair harder. It turns the next choice into a trial about character, not a plain choice about food.

The National Weight Control Registry points in a quieter direction. Rena Wing, James Hill, and the long-term maintainers are not a story about one miracle food. They are a story about feedback and routine: monitor weight, plan meals, reduce cues, avoid all-or-nothing rules, maintain activity. Monitoring is feedback before shame gets a vote. The scale is not a judge when it is used well. The meal plan is not a cage when it keeps hunger from making every choice fresh. The rule is not "never want food." The rule is "do not make hunger negotiate with food all day."
breakdown.fullRead:
Oprah Winfrey made this problem public in a way no lab sheet could. In 1988, the wagon of fat episode put weight loss before a television audience. Later public weight cycling made the lesson harder and more useful. Money, help, fame, and ambition did not make food a simple willpower test.

That matters for you when a plan starts to sound like a moral trial. If Oprah Winfrey could struggle in public, then private struggle is not proof that you are lazy. It may mean the setup is asking too much from restraint. Food cues wait in the fridge, in the app, at the deli counter, and in the message that says cake is in the lobby. Hunger arrives with its own lawyer. Shame then tries to act like a coach.

The stricter rule is tempting because it feels clean. No sugar. No snacks. No exceptions. A clean rule can help when it lowers cues and gives you fewer choices. The exception arrives when one ordinary meal, one party, or one tired night breaks the rule. If the rule has no repair path, it does not protect you. It hands the rest of the day to the lapse.

Frequent weighing has the same rule-and-exception shape. For some people, a calm scale check shows drift while repair is still small. The exception arrives when the number becomes a verdict. A useful scale asks what changed. A punishing scale asks what you are worth. If the second voice is the only one you hear, the first repair is to make the record calmer, not to make the shame louder.

This is why the useful system is dull on purpose. You monitor weight when that helps you catch drift early. You record enough to see patterns without turning each meal into a courtroom. You plan meals while calm. You move tempting food out of sight when you can. You keep activity as a routine, not as payment for guilt. None of this has the drama of a wagon on television. It works because it lowers the number of fights your tired self must win.

The rule also has a human cost. If you count cues before you restrict, you give up the fantasy that the right mood will carry you. Dylan feels that cost in the recreation center lobby when he closes the vending app and eats the breakfast he packed. He misses the quick thrill of choosing whatever he wants. He also avoids the later trial where hunger, shame, and a glowing snack photo all get a vote. A food plan costs a little freedom up front. The trade is not heroic. It is plain: fewer dramatic choices, more ordinary ones you can repeat.

examples.title: Clara Names the Broken Rule
examples.scenario: Participant Clara's tray drawer sticks halfway out of the lab cart during the preload block in the tasting room, and the cups rattle while Irene waits. In C. Peter Herman and Janet Polivy's restrained eating session, Clara has already swallowed the preload. Clara says, "I broke the rule." Irene nods toward the desserts: "So the rule is gone?"
examples.whatToDo: Clara names the thought before she eats more. Irene helps her separate the preload from the next bite, so counterregulation does not get to turn one event into a whole-day verdict.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows how restrained eating can snap when the rule has no repair path. A lapse needs a next step, not a fresh permission slip.

examples.title: Ophelie Reads the Scale
examples.scenario: The scale display blinks twice before Ophelie can slide it back under the sink. During a National Weight Control Registry follow-up, she starts to call the number proof that weighing is cruel. Then she hears her own mistake: Rena Wing and James Hill tracked long-term maintainers to study feedback, not self-punishment.
examples.whatToDo: Ophelie stops mid-reach and leaves the scale where she can use it calmly. She writes the number as feedback, then plans breakfast instead of arguing with herself.
examples.whyItMatters: Frequent self-weighing can help when it catches drift early. The recovery is in how Ophelie reads the number: signal first, shame last.

examples.title: Shirley's Post-Show Memo
examples.scenario: Producer Shirley's pen pauses above the word triumph after the taping, then she crosses it out inside the post-show office. Post-show memo, Oprah Winfrey 1988 wagon of fat episode: do not sell the television audience a fairy-tale ending. The public weight cycling that follows may show a harder truth: resources can help and still not erase food's daily pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Shirley sends a memo that cuts the victory language and asks for follow-up framing. She keeps Oprah Winfrey's struggle tied to food cues, biology, and public pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo protects the reader from blame. If fame and help do not remove the problem, relapse needs systems before shame.

examples.title: Lydia and Dylan Split Lunch
examples.scenario: Sliding her gym bag against the recreation center lobby wall before Saturday exercise class, maintainer Lydia skips breakfast so the day will feel clean. Dylan keeps his cereal cup and walking log before class. In the National Weight Control Registry pattern tracked by Rena Wing and James Hill, long-term maintainers lean on repeatable routines. Lydia spends lunch bargaining; Dylan eats what he planned.
examples.whatToDo: Lydia treats restraint as a fresh fight and loses the morning to hunger. Dylan treats breakfast, movement, and logging as ordinary rails, so lunch needs less willpower.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast keeps maintenance plain. The registry lesson is not sudden motivation; it is repeatable feedback before hunger gets loud.

examples.title: Alexander Keeps Repair Alive
examples.scenario: Alexander's pencil skips across the preload log when the dessert cart bumps the lab table. In C. Peter Herman and Janet Polivy's restrained eating session, Clara says, "I blew the rule, so why pretend?" Alexander answers, "That is counterregulation talking. A rule that dies after one bite is not restraint; it is a fuse."
examples.whatToDo: Alexander asks Clara to call the preload one event, not a verdict. He writes a repair path beside the dessert choice so restrained eating does not burn down.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk fits the rule-meets-exception problem. Strict restraint helps until a small break makes the rule fail. The reframe keeps repair alive.

examples.title: Irene Teaches the Harder Case
examples.scenario: The seminar slot is closing fast, and Irene still has one learner stuck on Oprah Winfrey's 1988 wagon of fat episode. "So money solves it until discipline fails?" the student asks. Irene uses the television audience and later public weight cycling to teach the harder case: support can help and still not remove daily food pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Irene has the class say the missing sentence out loud: resources reduce some barriers, but hunger, cues, and public weight cycling keep creating choices.
examples.whyItMatters: When support is visible, you may read regain as weak character. Oprah Winfrey's public cycling pushes you toward systems before blame.

questions.prompt: Dylan says, "I will handle sweets the way people handle cigarettes: never touch the category again." What does his response miss?
choices: He needs a stricter public promise around desserts.
He needs disgust to make the food category fade.
He still has to eat, so control needs moderated choices.
questions.explanation: Food control differs from abstinence because eating keeps returning. Dylan needs a plan for repeated moderated choices, not a vow that acts as if food can leave life.

questions.prompt: Clara drinks the preload, calls the diet blown, and reaches for more samples. Which reading best fits that sequence?
choices: The small lapse has sharpened restraint for the next choice.
The preload has removed hunger from the food decision.
The broken rule is giving the lapse permission to grow.
questions.explanation: Restrained eaters can overeat after a perceived violation. The tempting wrong read is that a lapse tightens control; here it weakens the rule.

questions.prompt: While reviewing her maintenance notes, Ophelie says, "The National Weight Control Registry proves the right mood keeps weight off." What does this claim miss?
choices: The registry points more to repeated monitoring and routine behavior.
The registry points more to one intense month of motivation.
The registry points more to a single best breakfast food.
questions.explanation: The registry pattern is maintenance by feedback and habits. Motivation may help, but the source fact supports repeated practices rather than one burst of resolve.

questions.prompt: Shirley avoids the scale for weeks because she wants to protect her mood. What is the strongest warning from the dieting evidence?
choices: Scale avoidance may keep the plan peaceful until a new diet starts.
A calm scale check may expose drift while repair is still small.
A scale number may matter only after the routine has failed.
questions.explanation: Frequent self-weighing can help some maintainers by making drift visible early. The near-miss is treating avoidance as protection when it may hide a small repair.

questions.prompt: Irene says, "If Oprah struggled after all that support, she must not have wanted it enough." What should her first correction be?
choices: Support does not remove biology, cues, or regain pressure.
Support matters only when the audience cannot see the goal.
Support works best when a public promise raises the stakes.
questions.explanation: Oprah Winfrey's public cycling separates dieting from simple laziness stories. Resources can help and still leave a hard control environment in place.

questions.prompt: A snack bowl stays beside Alexander's laptop while he writes. Before he chooses anything, he keeps looking over. What is already happening?
choices: The snack bowl is waiting for a deliberate food decision.
The snack bowl matters only if hunger is already strong.
The visible cue is raising attention before the choice.
questions.explanation: Visible cues can start desire before a deliberate choice. Alexander's attention is already being pulled, so the restraint demand has begun.

questions.prompt: After exercise class, Alexander asks why Lydia would pack lunch before she is hungry. Which answer best follows the food-control system?
choices: She chooses while calm instead of renegotiating with hunger.
She proves the planned meal is more authentic than craving.
She removes the need to notice food cues later.
questions.explanation: Preplanned meals reduce decision fatigue because the choice is made before hunger and cues get louder. The plan does not prove authenticity or remove every cue.

questions.prompt: After the dessert tray comes back, Clara says, "I ate the cookie, so I should feel awful enough to behave tomorrow." What does that line risk doing?
choices: It may make the next meal easier by raising concern.
It may turn one lapse into proof the plan is ruined.
It may keep hunger separate from the food decision.
questions.explanation: Shame can worsen dieting when it feeds all-or-nothing thinking. Clara may abandon repair because the feeling says the whole plan is spoiled.

questions.prompt: Lydia reaches her goal weight and wants to drop the routines that got her there. What is the most likely problem with that next move?
choices: The visible goal has made future routines less useful.
Food choices will keep arriving after the weight loss.
Maintenance now depends mainly on stronger restriction.
questions.explanation: Weight loss does not end the food environment. Long-term control still needs systems because meals, cues, and decisions keep showing up.

reviewCards.front: Why is dieting harder than habits based on full abstinence?
reviewCards.back: Food cannot leave life. You still have to eat, so the plan has to manage repeated choices, hunger, and cues instead of pretending the whole category can disappear.

reviewCards.front: How can one diet lapse lead to more eating?
reviewCards.back: A rigid rule can make a small lapse feel like total failure. Once the day feels ruined, the person may treat more eating as already permitted.

reviewCards.front: What did the National Weight Control Registry add to the dieting lesson?
reviewCards.back: It shifted attention from miracle foods and sudden drive to maintenance routines: feedback, breakfast in many reports, activity, and repeated habits that can be checked.

reviewCards.front: Why does Oprah Winfrey's public weight cycling matter here?
reviewCards.back: It makes the problem less moralistic. Fame, help, and ambition can coexist with regain, so the better question is how biology and cues keep testing the plan.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of the Sustainable food-control system?
reviewCards.back: The five parts are monitor weight, plan meals, reduce cues, avoid all-or-nothing rules, and maintain activity. Together they lower repeated willpower fights.

reviewCards.front: How would one sentence connect earned self-regulation (Ch 9) to Count Before You Restrict?
reviewCards.back: Ch 9 builds waiting and repair through structure. Count Before You Restrict applies the same idea to food by letting meals, cues, and monitoring carry more control.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice Count Before You Restrict when food starts to feel like a verdict. Count the cue, the hunger, or the shame before you tighten the rule. Then choose one routine that lowers the next fight: monitor weight, plan meals, reduce cues, avoid all-or-nothing rules, or maintain activity.

ifThenPlans.context: One bite makes the rest of the day feel ruined.
ifThenPlans.plan: If one bite feels like failure, then use Count Before You Restrict: tally it as one event and write the next ordinary meal.

ifThenPlans.context: A visible food cue keeps pulling your eyes back.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a cue keeps grabbing attention, then use Count Before You Restrict: mark one tally and move the cue out of easy sight.

ifThenPlans.context: Hunger is making a spontaneous meal sound wiser than it is.
ifThenPlans.plan: If hunger starts arguing for a fresh choice, then use Count Before You Restrict: count the cue and eat the meal chosen while calm.

ifThenPlans.context: The scale feels like a judge instead of feedback.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the scale feels like a verdict, then use Count Before You Restrict: count the gap since the last check and write one small repair.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, count each time hunger meets a visible food cue before you choose. Put one tally beside the cue, then name the next routine that would lower the fight.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person to flag when they hear you turn a food cue or lapse into a verdict this week. Compare notes once and choose one routine to make that moment smaller.

memorableLines.text: A brittle rule turns a bite into a verdict.
Monitoring is feedback before shame gets a vote.
A food plan costs a little freedom up front.
